doc.title: Onaje Allan Gumbs interviewed by Monk Rowe, New York City, New York, January 12, 2001

title: A musician's week and Vanessa Rubin recording his old song
summary: He describes a typical week, old compositions being recorded, and producing Vanessa Rubin, who recorded Autumn.

story.theme_name: Writing and arranging: how musicians compose
story.community_name: Writing, arranging and composing: how the music gets made

blocks.x: Tell me what a typical week is like for a musician like yourself in New York.

For me? Watching Jerry Springer. No. Sometimes it’s like that for a musician, you know, watching TV. A good week is getting calls from different people. A good week is hooking up a session with somebody, getting a call to go to Lebanon, getting a call to go to Japan. I haven’t written as much in recent years. I used to write music every day in high school. What’s happened now is that a lot of my old stuff is being recorded now.

Stuff that I wrote when I was fourteen, fifteen years old, is now being recorded. I present this tune to a person, oh, it’s a great tune. You know Vanessa Williams — Vanessa Williams — Vanessa Rubin, I produced her first album. Her first two albums. And she did a song of mine that I wrote when I was fifteen years old. The lyrics were written much later, but the song itself was written when I was fifteen. I played it for her, she loved it, it got reviewed in a CD magazine, the year-end review of CDs for that year. The © Hamilton College Jazz Archive -15-

reviewer somehow thought that my tune was a standard. He said well Vanessa recorded the standards, “Got the World on a String,” “Tenderly,” “Autumn” blah-blah. I said “Autumn,” that’s my song. First recording of the song. But he thought it was a standard, which made me feel very good. Because one thing that — you may get disagreement from people — but one thing that bothers me is that a lot of the cats now are not writing the new standards.
